question: How does the body normally keep its hormone levels balanced and in check?
explanation: Think of negative feedback as the body's natural thermostat or brake system. When hormone levels get too high, it signals the body to slow down production so everything stays balanced. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h1)

question: What is the main difference between endocrine and exocrine glands?

options.A: Endocrine glands use ducts to transport fluids to body surfaces.
options.B: Endocrine glands produce enzymes instead of chemical messengers.
options.C: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
options.D: Endocrine glands only function during physical stress.

explanation: Remember: Endocrine means 'ductless'—they release their hormones straight into nearby blood vessels. Exocrine glands (like sweat or salivary glands) use ducts to send their products to a surface. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h1)

question: Steroid hormones are primarily made from which building block?
explanation: Steroid hormones are lipids built from cholesterol! This fat-friendly makeup is actually what helps them easily slip right across cell membranes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h2)

question: Why do lipid-soluble (steroid) hormones need carrier proteins to travel through the blood?

options.A: To speed up their breakdown by the liver and kidneys
options.B: Because blood plasma is mostly water and they do not mix well
options.C: To help them actively destroy harmful pathogens in the blood
options.D: Because they are too large to pass through capillary walls

explanation: Oil and water don't mix! Since blood plasma is mostly water, these fat-based steroid hormones need a carrier protein to hitch a ride and travel safely through circulation. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h2)

question: What actually happens during 'hormone resistance' at the cellular level?

options.A: Target cells fail to respond properly to circulating hormones
options.B: The endocrine gland completely stops producing hormones
options.C: Kidneys filter out the hormone before it reaches tissues
options.D: Enzymes in the liver destroy the hormone too quickly

explanation: Even though the hormone is floating right there in the blood, the target cells ignore the signal—usually because their receptors are damaged or blocked. It's like having a key, but the lock is jammed! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h3)

question: A patient has high levels of a hormone in their blood, yet shows symptoms of a deficiency. What is going on?

options.A: Excessive clearance of hormones by the liver
options.B: Target cell receptor resistance or signal defect
options.C: An increase in total receptor number on cells
options.D: Complete destruction of the endocrine gland

explanation: This is a classic sign of hormone resistance! There's plenty of the hormone around, but the cells' receptors aren't responding to it, leading to deficiency symptoms anyway. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h3)

question: What is the primary cause of Type 1 diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.B: Gradual development of peripheral insulin resistance
options.C: Overproduction of glucagon by alpha cells
options.D: Excessive dietary intake of refined carbohydrates

explanation: In Type 1 diabetes, the body's immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the beta cells in the pancreas, meaning the body can no longer make insulin. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h4)

question: Which combination of health issues defines metabolic syndrome?

options.A: Frequent infections, joint pain, and low blood pressure
options.B: Dehydration, rapid heart rate, and high potassium levels
options.C: Central obesity, high blood pressure, and abnormal blood lipids
options.D: Chronic kidney failure, low body weight, and severe anemia

explanation: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of risk factors—belly fat, high blood pressure, and poor cholesterol/lipid numbers—that together raise the chance of heart disease. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h4)

question: Which of these is a classic sign that a patient might have hypothyroidism?

options.B: High resting heart rate or tachycardia

explanation: A sluggish thyroid slows down the body's metabolism and heat production. Because of this, hypothyroid patients often feel freezing cold even when everyone else is comfortable. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h5)

question: Why does Graves' disease cause hyperthyroidism?

options.A: The pituitary gland stops releasing any regulatory hormones
options.B: Dietary iodine levels become excessively high in the bloodstream
options.C: Thyroid tissue undergoes widespread autoimmune destruction
options.D: Antibodies mimic TSH and continuously stimulate the thyroid gland

explanation: In Graves' disease, rogue antibodies trick the thyroid by acting just like TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), forcing the gland to pump out way too much thyroid hormone. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h5)

question: What physical feature is most commonly seen in Cushing's syndrome?

options.A: Permanent low blood pressure and dehydration
options.B: Central obesity with a round 'moon face'
options.C: Dark bronze hyperpigmentation of the skin
options.D: Severe weight loss and profound muscle wasting

explanation: Too much cortisol changes how fat is stored in the body, leading to a characteristic round 'moon face' and extra weight packed around the trunk and upper back. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h6)

question: Why do patients with Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) often develop dark, pigmented skin?

options.A: The adrenal glands leak excess stored pigments directly into the blood
options.B: Dehydration causes the outer skin layers to thicken and darken
options.C: Poor kidney function traps waste products underneath the skin layers
options.D: The pituitary gland releases high amounts of ACTH, which stimulates melanin

explanation: When the adrenals fail to make enough cortisol, the brain panics and pumps out a flood of ACTH to try and wake them up. High ACTH accidentally triggers melanin (skin pigment) production too! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h6)

question: What is the main job of the parathyroid hormone (PTH)?

options.A: To stimulate the pancreas to release stored insulin
options.B: To store extra calcium directly inside the kidney tissues
options.C: To lower blood calcium by moving it into the bones
options.D: To raise blood calcium levels when they drop too low

explanation: When blood calcium gets dangerously low, PTH steps in to rescue it by pulling calcium out of the bones, saving it in the kidneys, and helping absorb more from food. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h7)

question: What would you expect to see in a patient experiencing acute low calcium (hypocalcemia) due to a parathyroid problem?

options.A: Sluggish reflexes and profound muscle weakness
options.B: High blood pressure and excessive urination
options.C: Rapid bone hardening and increased density

explanation: Calcium keeps our nerves calm and stable. When calcium drops too low, the nerves become super irritable and twitchy, causing painful muscle cramps and spasms. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h7)

question: Why do endocrine disorders often cause symptoms all over the body in different organs?

options.A: Endocrine glands are physically connected to every single organ in the human body
options.B: Hormones travel systemically through the bloodstream to reach many different target tissues
options.C: The liver automatically spreads hormone imbalances to the digestive tract
options.D: Hormone receptors are identical across all types of tissues and organs

explanation: Hormones are chemical messengers that travel far and wide through the bloodstream. If there's too much or too little of one, every organ that has receptors for it will feel the impact! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h8)

question: What is the most crucial nursing action when caring for a patient having a severe endocrine emergency like a thyroid storm?

options.A: Closely monitoring vital signs and supporting stable organ function
options.B: Withholding prescribed medications until lab results return
options.C: Restricting all fluid intake to prevent swelling and weight gain
options.D: Encouraging heavy physical exercise to burn off excess energy

explanation: Endocrine emergencies cause wild, dangerous shifts in vitals and metabolism. Keeping a close eye on vital signs and giving steady supportive care is always your top priority. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T13#GNS222_U2_T13_h8)
